We have carbon NMR peaks: 169.52, 132.43,130.27,129.30,126.70,126.66,123.57,43.30,26.29 ppm.

Methyl carbons typically around 10-30 ppm. Here we have peaks at 43.30 and 26.29. 43 ppm could be a carbon attached to heteroatom (e.g., carbonyl adjacent). 26.29 is typical methyl. Also maybe 43 is a methylene? But question: number of methyl (CH3) groups. Need to infer from carbon NMR: each methyl carbon gives a signal. We have one low-field methyl at 26.29. Could there be another methyl hidden? 43.30 maybe a carbon attached to carbonyl (e.g., acetyl CH3 appears ~30 ppm). Actually acetyl methyl (CH3-CO) appears around 30 ppm. 43 is higher, maybe a carbon attached to heteroatom like O-CH3 (methoxy) appears ~55 ppm. So 43 is maybe a CH2. So likely only one methyl.

But we could also get proton NMR to confirm. Let's get proton NMR.
